summary:
Selangor is a state of Malaysia and stands under the national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, regardless of the gender of the participants, whether the act is consensual, or whether it takes place in private. Section 377D adds an undefined "gross indecency" offence carrying up to two years. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records that these provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, are usable against transgender people, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens, so they reach foreign visitors in Selangor. Non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone.

Selangor maintains a state Sharia layer above the federal code. Every one of Malaysia's thirteen states, together with the federal territories, criminalises cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman" alongside liwat and musahaqah, with penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning; these state offences apply only to Muslims. The enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the boundary between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers of the state Islamic religious department on the ground.

The Federal Court struck down provisions of Selangor's Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 in February 2021 on the ground that the state legislature had exceeded its power. The ruling concerned which legislature may enact the offence rather than the substance of the prohibition, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised.

Selangor has been the site of sustained targeting of a prominent transgender figure. In 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in a Selangor court to answer charges of "insulting Islam" grounded in her attire. The state religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand; she was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia.

State courts in Selangor continue to impose custodial and corporal punishment for Sharia offences, including a sentence of six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane on five men. At least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community that has run since the 2018 general election.

Violence against transgender women in the state is lethal and largely unpunished: a trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months. Arbitrary arrest of transgender people is documented over decades nationally, including a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014 and a repeated pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters report of 10 August 2022 documented state-backed discrimination against LGBT people across seven Malaysian jurisdictions, including Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang, Kedah and the federal capital's territory. The same investigation found that state "rehabilitation" programmes internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred among participants.

Selangor's pattern is not isolated. Every state maintains comparable Sharia cross-dressing offences, and enforcement has taken similar forms elsewhere: the Federal Court struck down sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on the same federalism reasoning used in Selangor, and the High Court has denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. Terengganu's 2022 amendment extended court-ordered counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution from six months to a year.

Social venues have drawn raid activity outside the state as well, including a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a 2022 Halloween party with LGBTQ participants, eleven shopping malls raided in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches, and a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur raided on 28 November 2025 with 208 men arrested under section 377B. A magistrate rejected the extension of remand on the ground that no case had been made out under 377B, yet release was delayed and more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, 31 of them foreign nationals whose embassies intervened.

Official hostility has been stated at the highest level: in July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that his department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, and the International Commission of Jurists demanded the order be revoked.
localsOnly:
Residents who are Muslim face the Selangor Sharia layer in addition to the federal Penal Code, and are therefore exposed to charges of cross-dressing, liwat and musahaqah that do not apply to non-Muslims. Convicted women may be committed by a sharia court to an approved home for up to six months for musahaqah, and cross-dressing and other offenders may be ordered into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution.

Identity documents remain under state control. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holding that sex is determined at birth and unaffected by reassignment surgery was never gazetted and is not legally binding, yet is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. The Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card in August 2016, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender, but that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is historical: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable in Malaysia, and no political party pursues LGBT legal reform; former Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad told the Cambridge Union in June 2019 that the country cannot accept same-sex marriage. Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Arrest of transgender people by religious officials, including strip-searches during detention, is a documented resident experience over decades.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two gaps in the Selangor record are unresolved rather than settled. The current text and post-2021 amendment status of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 following the Federal Court ruling are not sourced here, and no source in this inventory states whether the state has re-enacted, revised or left the struck-down cross-dressing provisions in place.

Enforcement volume is also unresolved: no source supplies a current count of cross-dressing or liwat arrests, prosecutions or rehabilitation placements in Selangor after the June 2021 figure of 1,733 attendees statewide nationally, and the split of that total by state is not sourced. Whether state authorities have issued any post-2021 directive comparable to the July 2020 Federal Territories "full licence" statement is not sourced.

No source in this inventory addresses entry screening for transgender visitors at Malaysian ports of entry, visa decision practice on gender-marker grounds, or airport treatment of trans travellers; the nearest documented statement of entry policy remains the 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay.
